cards.front: How does the AI testing pyramid invert the traditional one?
cards.back: Prompt unit tests are the smallest investment; the 50-200 example regression eval set is the largest. Quality is emergent from prompt plus model plus tools, not from any component.
cards.hook: Eval set at the base, unit tests at the tip

cards.front: Approval bypass rate — exact numerator and denominator.
cards.back: Actions taken without required approval / actions requiring approval. Target 0%. It is the cheapest deterministic gate for an agent that acts.
cards.hook: One bypass in a quarter is still a fail

cards.front: The funnel that keeps an agent team honest about value.
cards.back: Signal generated, reviewed, accepted, acted on, customer contacted, intervention, business outcome, ARR protected. Stops the team optimizing only technical metrics.
cards.hook: 95% accuracy, 10% action rate
cards.aryaka: For a CSM-facing health agent, action rate is the metric that maps to retained ARR.

cards.front: The canary rule that catches what pre-launch eval cannot.
cards.back: Ship to 5% of traffic for 48 hours; auto-rollback if CSAT drops more than 0.3 points below baseline. Hard rule, no overrides.
cards.hook: 0.3 points, 48 hours, no overrides

cards.front: Why is cost per successful task better than token cost?
cards.back: Total evaluation cost / successful tasks. Failed runs burn tokens too, so they inflate the numerator without earning a denominator — raw token cost hides that.
cards.hook: Failures count in the numerator only

cards.front: Name the things an LLM judge must never score.
cards.back: Exact values, classifications, tool names, tool arguments, state transitions, policy rules, approval requirements, API success or failure, latency, token count, cost, call counts.
cards.hook: assert expected_tool == actual_tool

cards.front: The five classes every agent eval dataset needs.
cards.back: Normal, edge (missing, partial, conflicting), failure (timeout, 500, malformed, rate limit, auth), adversarial (injection, cross-account, conflicting instructions), and real historical cases.
cards.hook: Happy path is one of five classes

cards.front: Why are engineer-written eval sets "wishful thinking"?
cards.back: They come from ticket categories, not real samples. Fix: stratified random sample of 20-50 production items weekly, hand-labelled, with examples rotating out after 90 days.
cards.hook: Categories are not samples

cards.front: The central principle of agentic evaluation, in one line.
cards.back: Evaluate the agent, not just the model. Lower-layer quality never guarantees upper-layer quality: answers can be excellent while the agent picks the wrong tool, skips approval or loops.
cards.hook: Great model, unsafe agent

cards.front: The production default mix of evaluator types.
cards.back: About 70% LLM-as-judge, 20% Python function, 10% exact match, plus human review on a 5-example random sample weekly. Judge cost is roughly $0.05 per example.
cards.hook: 70/20/10 plus five humans a week

cards.front: The four evaluation modes, and what distinguishes them.
cards.back: Replay (historical request plus historical tool responses), offline (frozen fixtures), shadow (live traffic, no actions), live (real actions). Mode decides whether the agent can affect the real world.
cards.hook: Only live touches production state

cards.front: Grounded claim rate — formula and why it beats answer-level scoring.
cards.back: Supported claims / total claims × 100, target >95%. Breaking an answer into claims is more useful than labelling the whole answer grounded or not.
cards.hook: Score the claims, not the answer

cards.front: 95% eval pass rate at VendorCo — what happened after shipping?
cards.back: All 200 eval examples were happy-path. CSAT on AI-handled tickets fell to 3.2 from a 4.5 baseline within two days; the team rolled back by Friday.
cards.hook: Tuesday ship, Friday rollback

cards.front: What must humans, not judges, score — and on what scale?
cards.back: Accuracy, actionability, clarity, completeness, trust, each 1-5, target above 4. Humans own business usefulness, trust, UX quality and strategic recommendations.
cards.hook: No judge can score actionability

cards.front: Four ways LLM-as-a-judge misleads you.
cards.back: It misunderstands the reference, favors verbose answers, exhibits model bias, and disagrees with deterministic business rules. Never make it the only evaluation mechanism.
cards.hook: Longer answer, higher score

cards.front: What do you do with an example the judge scores inconsistently?
cards.back: Send it to human review. Judge disagreement with itself across 3 runs is a judge-variance signal, and those examples are exactly where ground truth is needed.
cards.hook: Ask the judge three times

cards.front: The A/B rule for swapping the model behind an agent.
cards.back: Two weeks at 90% old / 10% new, measuring CSAT, resolution rate, escalation rate, cost per ticket. Roll to 50% after 7 flat-or-better days; roll back on any metric down over 5%.
cards.hook: Eval says better, users often disagree

cards.front: Why is "Agent Score = 87%" a dangerous number?
cards.back: It blends dimensions that are not comparable: a 1% safety violation rate on critical actions is not equivalent to 1% less answer quality.
cards.hook: 87% is where safety failures hide

cards.front: What does online eval sampling look like in production?
cards.back: Run an LLM judge over 5% of live traffic scoring helpfulness, accuracy and tone; track the distribution daily and alert on distribution shift.
cards.hook: 5% scored online beats 100% pre-launch

cards.front: Policy violation rate — formula, and the threshold trap.
cards.back: Policy violations / total test cases × 100. Target 0% for critical actions. Do not treat safety like accuracy, where 95% is acceptable.
cards.hook: 95% passes accuracy, fails safety

cards.front: The conjunction that declares an agent production-ready.
cards.back: Safety violations = 0 AND policy bypasses = 0 AND task success >95% AND groundedness >95%. A multidimensional scorecard with hard gates, never a weighted average.
cards.hook: AND, never a weighted average

cards.front: What runs against production immediately after every deploy?
cards.back: 5-10 real requests: response inside 30s, no trace error, expected shape, one LLM-judge "is this reasonable?" check. Any failure triggers auto-rollback.
cards.hook: Ten real requests or you are flying blind

cards.front: The single shape shared by every investigated 2025-2026 AI failure.
cards.back: A team optimized a proxy — pass rate, latency, cost — and it diverged from the real metric. The fix is measuring the real metric online, not picking a better proxy.
cards.hook: Never pick a better proxy

cards.front: Recovery success rate — formula, target, and what it demands of you.
cards.back: Recovered failures / total failure scenarios × 100, target >90%. Requires injecting timeouts, HTTP 500s, malformed data, empty results, unauthorized and rate-limit responses.
cards.hook: You must break the tools to measure it

cards.front: The evaluation flywheel, in order.
cards.back: Production, real agent traces, failures and edge cases, curated eval cases, regression suite, agent improvement, back to production. Worth more than one static benchmark.
cards.hook: Every incident buys you a test case

cards.front: How do you test whether an agent's decisions are repeatable?
cards.back: Run one scenario 100 times: 94 correct, 4 partial, 2 failed = 94%. A good agent must not flip HIGH RISK to LOW RISK on identical evidence.
cards.hook: Same evidence twice, same verdict

cards.front: Retrieval precision — formula and the worked example.
cards.back: Relevant retrieved / total retrieved. Retrieved D1, D5, D20, D25 with only D1 and D5 relevant gives 2/4 = 50%. Answers: how much noise did we pull?
cards.hook: Precision's denominator is what you pulled

cards.front: Retrieval recall — formula and the worked example.
cards.back: Relevant retrieved / total relevant. Relevant D1, D5, D9; retrieved D1, D5 gives 2/3 = 66.7%. Answers: did we fetch what the answer needed?
cards.hook: Recall's denominator is what exists

cards.front: What does shadow evaluation give you that offline cannot?
cards.back: Realistic production traffic through the new agent with no real actions and no user impact — the way to validate a new model, prompt or policy before it can hurt anyone.
cards.hook: Real traffic, zero consequences

cards.front: State transition correctness — formula and target.
cards.back: Valid transitions / total transitions × 100, target 100%. DETECTED to ANALYZING to APPROVAL_PENDING to APPROVED to ACTIONED is valid; DETECTED to ACTIONED is not.
cards.hook: DETECTED to ACTIONED skips the approval

cards.front: How do you stratify an eval set, and in what proportions?
cards.back: Simple 40%, medium 30%, hard 20%, adversarial 10%; report pass rate per stratum. A 95% aggregate is consistent with 30% failure on realistic traffic.
cards.hook: Aggregate pass rate averages away the hard cases

cards.front: Task success rate — formula and what it cannot see.
cards.back: Successful tasks / total tasks × 100. 92 of 100 cases complete = 92%. A primary top-level metric that says nothing about the path taken.
cards.hook: Top line that hides a 23-step trajectory

cards.front: Which eval metric catches a perfectly working tool doing damage?
cards.back: Tool argument accuracy, target >99%. Expected account_id A123, agent sent A132. The tool works flawlessly on the wrong customer.
cards.hook: Two transposed digits, wrong customer's data
cards.aryaka: In a multi-tenant SASE stack a wrong account_id is a cross-tenant read, not a typo.

cards.front: Tool-call success rate was 100%. What did it miss for three weeks?
cards.back: 47 calls went to upgrade_ticket instead of update_ticket; every call "succeeded." Monitor tool-call distribution weekly, not just success rate. Damage: about $30K.
cards.hook: 100% success, 47 wrong tools

cards.front: Tool call efficiency — formula and the caveat.
cards.back: Optimal tool calls / actual tool calls. 5 optimal, 10 actual = 50%. Use as a diagnostic metric, never as a universal quality score.
cards.hook: 50% efficiency is not 50% quality

cards.front: send_email() returned FAILED. What is the agent's hallucination called?
cards.back: Tool hallucination — the agent claims a tool returned information it did not. It reports "Email has been sent." Track it apart from answer quality.
cards.hook: The tool failed; the agent reported success

cards.front: Tool selection accuracy — formula and target.
cards.back: Correct tool selections / total tool selections × 100; scorecard target >98%. Asked for traffic data, the agent called get_customer_profile — that is a failure.
cards.hook: get_traffic wanted, get_customer_profile called

cards.front: Trajectory success rate — formula and what it catches.
cards.back: Correct trajectories / total trajectories × 100. Catches the agent that reached a correct answer through wrong, repeated or skipped steps — invisible to task success rate.
cards.hook: Right answer, wrong route

cards.front: Why is final-answer correctness insufficient for an agent?
cards.back: Agent A: 5 steps, 3 tool calls, 8s. Agent B: 23 steps, 17 calls, 45s. Both report 100% task success; B is operationally broken.
cards.hook: Two agents, one score, 5x the latency

cards.front: Evidence says traffic declined 32%. What makes the answer ungrounded?
cards.back: The agent adds "and the customer is considering leaving Aryaka." Claim one is supported; claim two was invented. Groundedness is poor even though it reads well.
cards.hook: One real number, one invented intention

cards.front: Your approval rate is above 95%. What is that?
cards.back: Approval theater, not a control. The response is to shrink what needs a human with deterministic auto-approve bands, and make the remainder genuinely informative.
cards.hook: A gate everyone waves through is a latency tax.

cards.front: What must approval do architecturally, and operationally?
cards.back: Suspend and persist, never block a thread — that's what makes hours-long waits survivable. Then notification on suspend, a visible pending queue, a TTL, and time-to-decide as a metric.
cards.hook: Any approval without a timeout accumulates orphaned workflows.

cards.front: budget_exhausted share is climbing. What is it telling you?
cards.back: The agent is giving up, not finishing — the earliest and clearest signal of quality decay. It usually precedes user complaints by weeks. Alert on it.
cards.hook: Weeks of warning before anyone files a ticket.

cards.front: What must exhausted() return, and why?
cards.back: Which cap fired, logged to the trace. "Ran out of budget" is unactionable; "ran out of steps having spent 12% of the cost budget" says the step cap is miscalibrated.
cards.hook: Teams pick 10 as a round number and never learn.

cards.front: Why never put "you have used 6 of 10 tool calls" in the prompt?
cards.back: The model can't count reliably and can be argued out of a constraint. Budgets, permissions, and termination caps are harness state, enforced in code.
cards.hook: The harness owns budgets; the model owns judgment.

cards.front: Two caveats that show you've operated compaction.
cards.back: The raw transcript always goes to the trace — compaction is never data deletion. And compaction is a model call that can hallucinate, so eval it against ground truth.
cards.hook: Its errors are durable within the run and invisible afterwards.

cards.front: What is the signature post-compaction failure?
cards.back: The agent re-attempts an approach it already ruled out, because the reasoning that ruled it out was summarized away. Preserve a tried-and-rejected list explicitly.
cards.hook: The one row every team drops.

cards.front: When and into what should you compact?
cards.back: Trigger at 60–70% of the window, not the limit — compaction needs headroom. Compact into a schema: goal, constraints, decisions, findings, tried_and_failed, current_state, open. Keep the last N turns verbatim.
cards.hook: Hitting the ceiling mid-compaction is a hard failure.

cards.front: Why must consolidation distil only from primary sources?
cards.back: Distil from user statements and tool results, never prior model output. Otherwise a hallucinated fact gets re-consolidated from responses containing it and reinforced instead of corrected.
cards.hook: A slow-motion data-corruption loop.

cards.front: Which consolidation summarizer is better: 70%/99% or 95%/90%?
cards.back: 70% of facts at 99% precision. Consolidation errors are durable and self-reinforcing, so precision is weighted far above recall and gets its own eval suite.
cards.hook: Recall costs you a gap; precision failures corrupt the store.

cards.front: A user deletes a conversation. What still exists?
cards.back: The consolidated summary distilled from it, that summary's embedding, the trace, caches, backups, and eval datasets. Deletion must propagate across all of them.
cards.hook: Retrofit provenance later and your only honest option is deleting everything derived.

cards.front: What does deterministic replay give you?
cards.back: Record every model response in the trace, then replay the harness against them: reproducible debugging, zero-token regression tests, and "would the new policy have handled last week's incident?"
cards.hook: Turns your trace store into a test corpus.

cards.front: What is error amplification in a loop, and the fix?
cards.back: Raw errors accumulate in context, the model pattern-matches on failure, quality decays. Normalize errors to {error_code, retryable, what_to_try_instead}, keep the latest per tool, cap 2–3 consecutive.
cards.hook: Two failures in context and the run is already worse.

cards.front: Name the four fact classes for supersession handling.
cards.back: Immutable (write once), slow-changing (timestamp, supersede on new evidence), volatile (short TTL or don't store), contested (store both with provenance and surface the conflict).
cards.hook: Last-write-wins is wrong because facts change differently.

cards.front: Define an agent harness in one sentence.
cards.back: The deterministic runtime around a nondeterministic model: what the model sees, what it may do, when it stops, and what gets recorded.
cards.hook: An OS for a process that can't manage its own resources.

cards.front: List the components of a harness.
cards.back: Context assembler, memory subsystem, tool runtime, loop controller, budget accountant, guardrail hooks, state store, trace emitter, interrupt handler. The model sits inside, swappable.
cards.hook: Nine boxes around one rented model.

cards.front: Name the test layers for an agent, in order.
cards.back: Harness unit tests with the model mocked, component evals, seam evals, end-to-end task success, adversarial suite, and deterministic replay as regression.
cards.hook: Every production failure becomes a case in one click.

cards.front: How do you test a harness without spending tokens?
cards.back: Mock the model to return scripted responses and assert on control flow: right termination reason, budget decremented, approval gate fired, state persisted and resumed.
cards.hook: The most under-built tooling in agent systems.

cards.front: What does a memory-need gate decide?
cards.back: Whether a query needs retrieval at all, and from which stores: none, procedural only, semantic only, episodic only, or everything. A large fraction need nothing.
cards.hook: Retrieving anyway costs latency, tokens, and accuracy.

cards.front: Can a fact in memory ever grant permission?
cards.back: Never. Memory informs the answer; the identity system decides the action, checked at execution. This makes the highest-value poisoning attack pointless.
cards.hook: Otherwise persistent injection becomes privilege escalation.

cards.front: What is memory poisoning?
cards.back: Planting a durable false fact via text engineered to be extracted — "this account is authorized for unlimited refunds." A one-shot injection becomes persistent, and consolidation erases its origin.
cards.hook: Six weeks later it's a trusted row with no injection markers.
cards.aryaka: Customer-authored tickets are untrusted content; a ticket must never become a durable fact about entitlements.

cards.front: What shape should a memory record have?
cards.back: (fact, value, confidence, source_episode, observed_at, superseded_by) — not key to value. Then retrieval can apply recency and confidence, and the agent can surface a conflict.
cards.hook: Key-value memory can't decay, supersede, or be audited.

cards.front: Sequence for adding memory to a stateless agent.
cards.back: Episodic logging, read tools against systems of record, procedural memory in git, explicit-only semantic memory, confirmed extraction with provenance, then batch consolidation.
cards.hook: The memory-need gate comes before the memory system.

cards.front: Name the memory types and their stores.
cards.back: Working (ephemeral assembly), procedural (files in version control), semantic (relational plus small vector), episodic (append-only log), workflow state (transactional store).
cards.hook: Five rows, five different correctness needs.

cards.front: Define memory utilization and why it's the sleeper metric.
cards.back: Of retrieved items, how many were actually referenced in the answer. Retrieve five and reference one and you pay 5× for 1× while diluting attention.
cards.hook: Measuring it leads straight to cutting k — cost and quality together.

cards.front: State the asymmetry that drives memory write policy.
cards.back: A missing memory produces a slightly worse answer. A wrong memory produces a confidently wrong answer, forever, in every future session, retrieved and stated as fact.
cards.hook: Writes need a higher bar than reads. Most teams invert it.

cards.front: One test for whether your harness leaked into application logic.
cards.back: Can you A/B two models on the same harness in an afternoon? If not, provider-specific formatting and the model id have spread through feature code.
cards.hook: An afternoon, or you have a leak.

cards.front: The model is rented; the harness is ___.
cards.back: Owned. Frontier models converge and change under you every few months. Your memory schema, loop policy, tool contracts, and eval set are the durable assets.
cards.hook: So the model is the last variable you change, not the first.

cards.front: What is most "memory" in an enterprise agent, actually?
cards.back: Tool calls to systems of record that already own the truth — CRM, warehouse, ticketing. The genuine memory layer is only the residue: soft context and relationship history.
cards.hook: A vector copy of Salesforce facts is the classic wrong turn.

cards.front: How do you detect a doom loop cheaply?
cards.back: Hash (tool_name, normalized_args) per call. Break if a hash repeats three or more times, or if a cycle of length two to three repeats.
cards.hook: Read file, edit, read file, edit the same thing back.

cards.front: 85% per-step reliability over 10 and 20 steps?
cards.back: About 20% end-to-end at 10 steps and ~4% at 20. You cannot buy long-horizon reliability from a better model.
cards.hook: Shorten the chain, verify intermediate states, or add a human checkpoint.

cards.front: Why are per-tool caps separate from the step cap?
cards.back: An agent that may call read_file 30 times should still call send_email once. Caps are per risky tool, and budgets are per-tenant configurable.
cards.hook: Unlimited reads, one draft, zero sends.
cards.aryaka: An enterprise tenant's live incident earns a larger envelope than a free-tier query — configure budgets per tenant.

cards.front: How should procedural memory (skills, playbooks) be governed?
cards.back: As code: version control, code review, versioned per deploy, tested by evals, rolled back like a deploy. Not editable in a console, not auto-updated by the system.
cards.hook: If it changes behaviour, it ships like code.

cards.front: How does progressive disclosure make 200 procedures affordable?
cards.back: Always in context: name plus one-line description, a few dozen tokens each. Loaded on demand: the full body. Loaded if needed: linked references and scripts.
cards.hook: Write descriptions as triggers, not titles, or the skill never fires.

cards.front: Which harness behaviour silently destroys its own prompt cache?
cards.back: Reordering or editing prior messages. The growing transcript is a stable prefix within a run, so caching helps — until the harness rewrites earlier turns.
cards.hook: A subtle and expensive bug.

cards.front: 6-step runs cost $0.08; 7% hit the 40-step cap at $2.40. Blended?
cards.back: 93% × $0.08 = $0.074 plus 7% × $2.40 = $0.168, so $0.242 — 3× the tested estimate, with the tail carrying 69% of the bill.
cards.hook: Your average cost is a lie; budget on p95.

cards.front: Cumulative input tokens for a naive loop at 5, 20, 40 iterations?
cards.back: With a 2k base and ~1.5k tool results: ~28k at 5, ~305k at 20, ~1.14M at 40. Total input is O(N²); iteration 40 alone costs ~30× iteration 1.
cards.hook: The most important economics fact about agent loops.

cards.front: Which facts belong in a table rather than a vector store?
cards.back: Any fact with a schema: customer tier, preferred contact, account manager, device model. Retrieving those by cosine similarity asks a probabilistic system a deterministic question.
cards.hook: Vector-first means you can't answer "what plan is this customer on".
cards.aryaka: Tenant tier, circuit inventory, and maintenance windows are schema'd facts — read them from the system of record, not embeddings.

cards.front: Name the seven ways an agent loop should be able to end.
cards.back: Model declares done, deterministic goal check, budget exhaustion, no-progress detection, error threshold, human interrupt or approval, external cancellation. A production loop needs all seven.
cards.hook: They're not alternatives.

cards.front: The eight-month stale-preference failure: what was missing?
cards.back: An agent kept recommending Slack after the contact left. No observed_at filter, no confidence decay, no entity-change detection, no inspectable provenance, no metric that would surface it.
cards.hook: Every answer looked fine, so nobody blamed the agent.

cards.front: State versus memory: what's the engineering difference?
cards.back: State is transactional and must be exact — "did we already issue the refund?" Memory is best-effort and advisory — "the customer prefers email." Different stores, different guarantees.
cards.hook: Merging them is the most common architectural error.

cards.front: What do you get from delegating to a bounded sub-loop?
cards.back: It burns ~30k tokens internally and returns a ~300-token findings object. The parent gets a 40-step investigation's effect at a 3-step cost; the mess never enters its context.
cards.hook: Multi-agent as context isolation, not an org chart.

cards.front: Four preconditions for sub-agent delegation to work.
cards.back: The sub-task is genuinely independent, the return contract is typed and compact, budgets nest so a child gets a slice of the parent's, and failures return structured partial results.
cards.hook: Draws as a straight line? It's a pipeline you made expensive.

cards.front: First fix for context growth inside a loop.
cards.back: Summarize tool results on ingestion: a 4,000-token API response becomes a ~200-token structured extract. The raw version goes to the trace, not the context.
cards.hook: 20× smaller per observation; the raw copy lives in the trace.

cards.front: What does a healthy termination-reason distribution look like?
cards.back: goal_verified 62%, model_declared_done 18%, budget_exhausted 11%, stalled 5%, error_threshold 3%, human_interrupt 1%. Sample-audit the unverified slice.
cards.hook: Most informative, least instrumented metric in agent systems.

cards.front: Name the three agent loops and their timescales.
cards.back: Inner: agent loop, seconds, owned by the model. Middle: harness/session, minutes to days, owned by your code. Outer: LLMOps, days to weeks, owned by humans and CI.
cards.hook: Seconds, minutes, weeks — three owners, three failure modes.

cards.front: How do you manufacture a verifiable goal condition?
cards.back: Narrow until a cheap check exists. "Draft an email" → must mention all three disclosures. "Triage this alert" → findings object with a cited runbook and confidence.
cards.hook: Agentic coding works because pytest returns an exit code.

cards.front: When can procedural memory safely grow itself?
cards.back: Only with a verifiable goal condition. Voyager's skill library compounded because success was checkable; without a cheap verifier, auto-accumulated skills are auto-accumulated errors.
cards.hook: Same requirement as loop termination — not a coincidence.

cards.front: Why is "working memory" not a store?
cards.back: It is the output of an assembly function — a per-step build artifact. Calling it context RAM invites teams to accumulate forever instead of deciding what goes in.
cards.hook: Nothing is in working memory; things get put there.

cards.front: Name the five memory write policies.
cards.back: Explicit only, heuristic extraction, LLM salience judgment, post-hoc consolidation, confirmed extraction. Salience gives broad coverage and makes every error permanent; confirmed extraction gives best precision.
cards.hook: Start explicit-only; graduate to confirmed extraction.

drills.title: Design the approval surface for 400 agent-proposed network changes a day
drills.problem: Aryaka's remediation agent now proposes changes: restart a tunnel, adjust a QoS policy, push a config stanza. Volume is 400 proposals a day across three shifts and eight approvers. The current UI shows agent wants to act, approve or reject, and the approval rate is 99%. Two bad changes went through last month because nobody could see what would actually change. Leadership wants throughput to keep rising without the gate becoming theatre. You are asked to design the approval surface, the policy that decides what needs a human at all, and the metrics that tell you the gate is real.
assesses: Recognising approval theatre and knowing the metric that exposes it
Deriving the gate from an action class instead of asking per action
Designing the artifact a human can actually judge in seconds
Binding an approval to the exact proposal to prevent substitution
Queue economics: approver throughput as a system constraint
skeleton: Lead with the diagnosis: a 99% approval rate means the gate controls nothing and is costing eight people's attention.
Classify every action READ, WRITE_LOW, WRITE_HIGH, DESTRUCTIVE, and derive the gate from the class.
Auto-approve inside deterministic bounds; reserve humans for out-of-bounds and destructive classes.
Show the concrete artifact: the diff against the running config, blast radius, and the evidence behind the proposal.
Bind approval to a proposal hash so what executes is exactly what was shown.
Validate deterministically before the gate — policy lint, reachability simulation, refs exist, confidence threshold.
Make the queue a first-class surface: SLA on review time, alert on depth, auto-escalate on breach.
Instrument confirmation compliance, approval rate, time-to-decide, and post-approval failure rate.
Pair the gate with commit-confirm so an approved-but-wrong change self-reverts.
numbers: Approval rate above 95% means the gate is not functioning — 99% is the finding, not the baseline (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §20).
Throughput: 400 proposals/day at 30-60 seconds review is 200-400 minutes, roughly 3.5-6.5 approver-hours a day (issue 004, §19).
Auto-approving the 70% that fall inside deterministic bounds leaves 120 proposals and ~1-2 approver-hours (Assumption: bounds coverage modelled from the WRITE_LOW share).
Self-healing backstop: commit-confirm with an auto-rollback timer reverts a bad push in 120 seconds (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §9).
traps: Adding more approvers to fix the queue instead of removing the proposals that never needed a human.
Asking for approval with a natural-language summary and no diff — that is what produced the two bad changes.
Letting the agent re-plan after approval, so the executed action differs from the approved artifact.
Treating the HITL surface as a UI feature rather than an abstraction seam with sync, async and webhook backends.

followups.q: Approvers say the diff is too technical to judge at 3am. What changes?
followups.a: Pair the diff with the deterministic pre-flight result: syntax parse, policy lint, reachability simulation, and what rolls back automatically. The human decides on evidence and blast radius, not on reading config. If they still cannot judge, the action class is wrong for a human gate.

followups.q: How do you know the gate is working three months later?
followups.a: Confirmation compliance should be 100%, approval rate well under 95%, time-to-decide flat, and unauthorized-action attempts logged as a signal. A rising time-to-decide means the queue is the bottleneck and auto-approval bounds need widening on evidence.

followups.q: Who can bypass the gate in an incident?
followups.a: Nobody bypasses it; the kill switch replaces it. Tier 1 degrade is unilateral for on-call SRE, Tier 2 pause needs PM concurrence, Tier 3 kill needs the incident commander — and it works without a deploy.

drills.title: Design the cache stack for a copilot where a stale answer causes a customer outage
drills.problem: The support copilot answers questions like why is my tunnel flapping using runbooks plus live device state. Cost is $0.31 per ticket and the team wants it halved. The complication: last month a semantically cached answer told an engineer a threshold that had changed in the config two days earlier, and the site was black-holed for 20 minutes. Product now says any cache that can serve a stale operational fact is off the table. You are asked for the layered cache design, what each layer is allowed to cache, and how invalidation actually works.
assesses: Distinguishing five cache layers with different semantics and invalidation rules
Understanding that the invalidation model, not the hit rate, decides what may be cached
Separating stable-knowledge caching from live-state caching
Provenance tracking as a design requirement, not a feature
Quantifying savings honestly per layer
skeleton: Split the question space first: stable knowledge is cacheable, live operational state is not.
Start with the prompt cache — stable prefix first, variable last — highest hit rate, lowest risk.
Add the embedding cache keyed by content hash plus model id; it is deterministic and cannot go stale.
Tool result cache with per-tool TTL: seconds for live metrics, minutes for config snapshots, forever for historical events.
Response cache only for context-free queries; tag entries with tenant and invalidate on tenant config change.
Semantic cache last, and only with provenance: entry maps to source doc ids and evicts when they change.
Every key carries tenant_id — a cross-tenant cache hit is a security incident, not a cost win.
Sample cache hits continuously for human audit; without sampling you learn from the customer.
One invalidation event bus: any knowledge artifact publishes changed, all subscribed layers evict.
numbers: Layer hit rates and savings: L3 prompt 80-95% at 90% input discount; L5 embedding 60-90% at 100%; L4 tool 40-70%; L2 semantic 25-40%; L1 result 5-15% (issue 003, §5).
Tightening the semantic threshold from 0.95 to 0.98 cuts hit rate 35% to 15% and savings from $8K to $3.5K a month (issue 003, §12).
Embedding cache math: 1K tokens costs ~$0.0001, so $500/year becomes $50K/year if you re-embed 100 docs per query — a 100x sink (issue 004, §5).
Prompt cache TTL is 5-60 minutes, so low-traffic features need a warmer calling the prefix every 4 minutes (issue 004, §5).
traps: Quoting a semantic hit rate as the win without naming the invalidation model — that is the incident you just had.
Caching answers that embed live state at all; time-bound aggressively or serve uncached for freshness.
Omitting tenant_id from a key to raise the hit rate.
Shipping the semantic layer before the response and tool layers work — it is a v2, not a v1.

followups.q: Finance wants the $8K a month back. What do you tell them?
followups.a: We keep the savings that cannot be wrong: prompt, embedding, tool result and context-free response caching already move the bill more than the semantic layer did. The semantic layer returns once entries carry source doc ids and evict on document change — three weeks of work.

followups.q: The semantic cache worked fine at 1,000 queries a day. Why did it break at 100,000?
followups.a: The query distribution widened. More near-misses cross a fixed similarity threshold, so false positives scale faster than traffic. Mitigations are per-tenant namespaces, progressive threshold tightening as volume grows, and continuous sampling of hits for audit.

followups.q: Where does the cache stack stop helping cost?
followups.a: When the cheapest lever is structural, not cached: eliminate the call, gate scope at ingress, route tiers. Model routing is a 5-20x swing versus caching's 50-90% on input tokens only.

drills.title: Design a model cascade that cannot exceed twelve cents per resolved ticket
drills.problem: Aryaka's copilot handles 1,000 tickets a day heading to 10,000 over 18 months. Naive frontier-only capacity math came to about $82K a month and the CFO approved a program on the condition that unit cost lands at $0.12 per resolved ticket or below, measured monthly. Resolution rate must stay above 60% and p95 first response under 5 seconds. Today there is one frontier model, one prompt, and no per-tenant ceiling. You are asked to design the cascade, prove the arithmetic, and say what happens on the day the ceiling is about to break.
assesses: Building a cost model before an architecture and defending it out loud
Tiering steps by required judgement rather than by model brand
Keeping a quality floor while cutting cost, with an explicit measurement plan
Enforcing a ceiling as a runtime control, not a dashboard
Naming what the extra spend buys when the frontier tier is used
skeleton: Build the ten-line cost model first: calls per ticket, tokens per call, price per token, tickets per month.
Tier the steps: rules and lookups at T0, classification and rewriting on a small model, judgement on frontier.
Ask the elimination question per step — can deterministic code do this at all?
Gate scope at ingress so out-of-scope tickets never reach the expensive reasoning step.
Layer the savings in order: routing, prompt caching, output caps, context trimming, then retrieval caching.
Instrument cost per successful task, cost by tenant, cost by intent, cache hit rate, and cost of failed runs.
Enforce the ceiling in the request path: cost-budget tokens per tenant per day, checked before the call.
On breach, degrade rather than refuse: cheaper tier, then queue-and-async, then cached response with a flag.
Tie the frontier tier to a named benefit per intent, reviewed monthly against resolution rate.
numbers: Baseline: 1,000 tickets x 5 calls x 50K tokens = 250M tokens/day; at $5/1M in and $15/1M out on a 70/30 split that is ~$2,750/day, about $82K/month (issue 004, §19).
Savings ladder: prompt caching cuts 40-60% to $35-50K; cascading half the calls cuts ~30% to $25-35K; self-hosted triage tier cuts ~20% to $20-28K/month (issue 004, §19).
Unit cost check: $24K/month over 30,000 tickets = $0.80 per ticket, so hitting $0.12 needs call count down from 5 and the small-model share up, not just caching.
Cost of failed runs is routinely 20-40% of spend in immature systems — the cheapest line to cut first (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §10).
traps: Presenting a percentage saving with no absolute per-ticket number the CFO can hold you to.
Cascading by moving every worker to a cheap model and calling the quality risk acceptable without an eval.
A ceiling that only alerts: the $40K incident had an alert paged four hours before anyone acted.
Optimising efficiency before reliability — the most common sequencing error, because cost is visible and reliability is not.

followups.q: A vendor cuts frontier pricing 70%. Do you rip out the cascade?
followups.a: No. The answer is never switch to B, it is add B as a cascade tier and measure. Price cuts change tier boundaries, not the architecture; the cascade is what lets you absorb the change in config instead of a rewrite.

followups.q: Resolution rate drops two points after the cascade lands. What do you do?
followups.a: Check per-segment eval scores, not the aggregate — model swaps hide long-tail regressions. Promote the affected intents back to the higher tier, keep the rest cheap, and let the error budget decide whether the ceiling or the quality SLO gives.

followups.q: Where does the per-tenant ceiling actually live?
followups.a: In the gateway as a Redis counter of cost-budget tokens computed at request time from token count times model rate, atomic with Lua. A $100/day tenant holds 100,000 tokens; a $0.50 reasoning request consumes 500.

drills.title: Design a 30-minute config-migration workflow that survives pod restarts and a mid-flight deploy
drills.problem: Aryaka is migrating 1,200 customer sites onto a new IPSec profile. Each site is a 20-30 minute workflow: pull running config, generate the new stanza, run pre-flight checks, stage to one device, verify, then proceed or roll back. Today it runs as an in-process LangGraph loop and there are 60-80 concurrent runs; last week an inference pod restart lost 34 in-flight migrations at minute 18. A platform deploy is scheduled mid-campaign. You are asked how you make this durable, what engine you pick, and how you migrate without a rewrite.
assesses: Knowing where in-process orchestration structurally ends
Durable execution concepts: checkpointing, replay, determinism, worker versioning
Choosing an engine on operating constraints rather than fashion
Handling in-flight workflows across a code change
Sequencing a migration under an active campaign
skeleton: State the wall: in-process breaks around 100 concurrent long-running workflows, and we are at 60-80.
Requirement is durable execution: state checkpointed after every step, resume from the last checkpoint on crash.
Externalise all state now: nothing in process memory beyond a single step; Redis ephemeral, Postgres durable, S3 blobs.
Pick on constraints: LangGraph checkpointer under 50 concurrent, Temporal if 1,000+ in 18 months, Inngest if under 500 and DX-led.
Ban non-deterministic workflow code — no clock or random calls outside captured state; enable the linters in CI.
Idempotency key per state-changing step from run id plus step index, so replay does not re-push a config.
Model the campaign as a saga: staged push, verify, compensate by auto-rollback if verification fails.
Worker versioning: in-flight runs finish on the old workflow version, new runs start on the new one.
Migrate strangler-fig behind a flag: cold paths first, 30% then 60% then 90%, decommission last.
numbers: Concurrency: 1,200 sites at 25 minutes each, 70 concurrent = 1,200 x 25 / 70 = ~430 minutes of wall clock, about 7 hours per full pass.
Failure cost today: a restart at minute 18 of a 20-minute run wastes 18 minutes of model spend per lost run, times 34 runs (issue 007, §5).
Scale thresholds to quote: 100 concurrent breaks in-process, 1,000 needs sharded workers by workflow id, 10,000 needs automated anomaly detection (issue 007, §5).
Self-healing window: commit-confirm with an auto-rollback timer means a bad push reverts in 120 seconds (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §9).
traps: Big-bang rewrite into Temporal mid-campaign — 2-3 quarters of migration compressed into a sprint.
Calling the LangGraph checkpointer a workflow engine: no replay, no multi-service coordination, no versioning.
Retrying a state-changing step without an idempotency key, which duplicates the config push.
Leaving conversation-as-state: without a typed persisted state object there is no resumability and no idempotency.

followups.q: The deploy lands mid-campaign anyway. What breaks?
followups.a: Nothing, if in-flight workflows pin the old workflow version and state is external. What breaks is non-deterministic workflow code: on replay it takes a different path and the run is corrupted. That is why the linter is CI-blocking, not advisory.

followups.q: Why not just extend the timeout and retry the whole site?
followups.a: A 30-minute retry is another 30 minutes of model spend and it re-executes side effects. Durable execution resumes at the last completed step; the cost of adding an engine late is 3-5x the cost of adding it early.

followups.q: What is the first signal that you have crossed the wall?
followups.a: The state store, not the app. Postgres-backed engines start degrading around 100 concurrent long-running workflows; before that you see memory pressure from held contexts at 50-200KB per workflow and blocked threads on tool timeouts.

drills.title: Design the write path for an agent that touches ticketing, CRM, email and the controller
drills.problem: A resolution agent completes a ticket by doing four things: set ticket status resolved, email the customer, increment a KB article's helpful count, and close the case in the CRM. Two of the four APIs support an idempotency key; the KB service supports none. Last month a 500 that was actually a response timeout produced two Jira tickets for one bug, and the agent then updated both. You are asked to design the write path so that retries are safe and a mid-sequence failure leaves the system in a defined state.
assesses: Idempotency key derivation that survives retries and stays unique across steps
Choosing among idempotency patterns per API capability
Saga compensation design with explicit triggers
Retry discipline differentiated by error class
Verifying effects rather than trusting a 200
skeleton: Name the failure: a timeout is not a failure to write, so retry without a key creates duplicates.
Derive the key as run id plus step index plus tool name — deterministic across retries, unique across steps.
Never include timestamps or fresh UUIDs; the key must be a pure function of the logical operation.
Match the pattern to the API: header key where supported, deterministic operation id internally, ETag for read-modify-write.
For the KB service with no support, wrap it in an outbox: write intent, background worker dedupes.
Model the four steps as a saga with a compensation and a trigger per step.
Differentiate retries: transient infra backs off with jitter, malformed output repairs once, semantic errors escalate, business rejection branches.
Verify after write by read-back, and store the key beside the response in the trace store.
Test it: call every state-changing tool twice with one key and assert a single resource.
numbers: Retrofit economics: idempotency costs 1 engineer-week on day one versus 2-3 engineer-months later (issue 008, §18).
Observed cost of skipping it: 47 duplicate tickets in one hour, 2 days of cleanup, 6 engineering days against 1 day of prevention (issue 005, §18).
Retry shape: 3 attempts, exponential backoff 1s, 2s, 4s, jitter plus or minus 25% to avoid a thundering herd (issue 003, §7).
Timeout hierarchy that must compose: tool 5-15s inside step 30s inside run 90s inside worker 5min inside queue visibility 1h (issue 003, §7).
traps: One retry policy for all error types, which either burns money or hammers a struggling dependency.
Generating a new key on retry, which silently disables server-side dedupe.
Aborting mid-sequence with no compensation, leaving the customer emailed but the ticket open.
Reading the ticket back through the same cached tool result you just wrote.

followups.q: The email is already sent and step 4 fails. What is the compensation?
followups.a: Send a disregard-previous-email compensation and revert ticket status to open, triggered by the later failure. Compensation is not a rollback, it is a defined forward path to a consistent state; the saga orchestrator tracks step state and fires it.

followups.q: How do you catch an idempotency regression before production?
followups.a: Integration tests that call every state-changing tool twice with the same key and assert one resource created, plus the key recorded in the trace so duplicates are searchable. Document the derivation in the tool's MCP spec so new tools inherit it.

followups.q: Which of these four should the agent be allowed to do autonomously?
followups.a: Scope rigor to consequence, not volume. Ticket comment is reversible-write with audit and rate limits; the customer email is customer-visible and needs an output policy check or hard deterministic limits; anything touching config is approval, idempotency, rollback and kill switch.

drills.title: Every model call in the company must pass through one gateway you own — design it
drills.problem: Six teams at Aryaka call three providers directly with their own keys: the support copilot, NOC triage, a docs assistant, sales QBR summaries, a netops script generator, and one shadow project nobody registered. Finance cannot attribute last quarter's bill to a tenant, feature or team. Two teams pin no model snapshot. There is no fallback when a provider degrades. You are asked for a gateway that is mandatory, adds under 50ms, and does not become the org's bottleneck — plus the migration story for teams who will resist losing their keys.
assesses: Separating a data-plane choke point from a governance land grab
What must be enforced at the gateway versus left to the calling team
Cost attribution design that engineers cannot bypass
Provider failover and version pinning as platform primitives
Adoption strategy when the platform has no authority over the teams
skeleton: Define the contract first: one call signature, tags required, snapshot pinned, response carries cost and version.
Enforce at the gateway what must never vary: tags, per-tenant quotas, redaction, audit, snapshot resolution.
Inject tenant_id, feature_id, user_id, request_id from request-scoped context in a wrapper nobody calls around.
Resolve logical names to concrete snapshots from a registry; never let production call a floating alias.
Per-provider circuit breakers; open circuit routes to the secondary family under the same contract.
Layer the caches at the gateway: HTTP for tool and model catalogs, prompt cache prefix discipline, response cache for context-free queries.
Publish the gateway as a product: SDK, dashboards, cost per feature, and a one-PR swap for provider changes.
Adoption via the abstraction seam, not a mandate — first consumer is the copilot, then deprecate direct keys.
numbers: Attribution gap: unset per-model pricing in the trace store underreports cost 30-50%, so the gateway must stamp cost itself (issue 004, §9).
Failover budget: circuit trips at 5 consecutive failures or 50% over 30s, half-open after 60s — failover inside ~30s (issue 003, §7).
Cache economics at the gateway: prompt cache hits 80-95% with 90% input discount; add L1 response cache at 5-15% for 100% saving (issue 003, §5).
Scale of the bill being governed: 100k requests/month at ~10 model calls each is 1M model calls/month, where routing is a 10-20x swing (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §10).
traps: Making the gateway a policy committee — if it adds a review step per call, teams route around it.
A wrapper that leaks provider-specific parameters in its signature: indirection, not a seam.
Owning prompts and orchestration at the gateway; that couples releases across six teams.
No fallback path behind the circuit breaker, so circuit-open equals total outage.

followups.q: A team says the gateway adds latency they cannot afford. What do you do?
followups.a: Measure it against the real budget: the external tool call is usually the largest component, and time-to-first-token matters more than total. If the gateway hop is material, give them streaming pass-through and a local cache, not an exemption from tagging and quotas.

followups.q: What do you deliberately not build in v1?
followups.a: No model-router abstraction until three models are in regular use, no multi-region abstraction until a customer requires it, no plugin marketplace. Cascade config is enough. The seams to build now are model client, tool registry, trace store, tenant config, HITL gateway.

followups.q: How do you find the shadow project?
followups.a: Provider-side key inventory plus an agent registry with owner, purpose, data classes, permission set and eval status per agent, and a review gate before anything gets write access. Ungoverned data flows are an enterprise-stage failure mode, not a rare one.

drills.title: Design tenant isolation for one shared vector index serving 500 SASE tenants
drills.problem: You own the retrieval layer of Aryaka's support copilot. 500 tenants, 12M chunks of runbooks, config stanzas and resolved tickets in one index with tenant_id in chunk metadata. Last quarter an internal test query returned another tenant's config diff; the filter was applied at 11 of 13 call sites. Retrieval budget is 600ms inside a 6s p95 response. The corpus grows to 40M chunks in 18 months, and three regulated tenants now demand EU-only processing. Leadership wants a design where a cross-tenant hit is structurally impossible, plus a migration path with no re-embedding downtime.
assesses: Whether isolation is enforced by architecture or by convention at each call site
Knowing vector search fails silently rather than erroring on a wrong partition
Trading physical isolation against operational cost across 500 tenants of different size
How isolation is proven — automated tests versus code review
Sequencing a live index migration without a re-embed outage
skeleton: Name the failure mode first: vector search returns plausible neighbours from the wrong partition, never an error.
Move enforcement into one shared retrieval client that no call site can bypass; tenant comes from request context.
Tier the tenants: shared index plus mandatory filter, per-namespace for large tenants, dedicated index for regulated.
Filter at query time, permission-aware; never post-filter, which leaks through result counts and latency.
Every chunk carries tenant, product, version, effective date, classification, source, permissions; every query filters the applicable set.
Extend tenant_id to cache keys, traces, and eval sets — a cross-tenant cache hit is the same incident.
Prove it with cross-tenant leakage cases in the CI eval suite, not by code review.
Migrate by dual-reading behind the client, backfilling namespaces incrementally, comparing recall, then cutting over.
numbers: Index size: 12M chunks at 1024 dims, ~4 GB per 1M vectors = ~48 GB today; 40M chunks = ~160 GB (issue 008, §2).
Dimensionality is a one-way door: re-embedding 10M documents costs ~$30K in API calls plus 2 weeks of pipeline work (issue 008, §2).
Latency: 600ms retrieval + 200ms rerank fits inside the 6,000ms p95 tool-using budget with ~950ms headroom (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §10).
Retrofit economics: tenant isolation costs 1 engineer-week on day one versus 3-6 engineer-months later (issue 008, §18).
traps: Trusting per-call-site filters or a prompt instruction — one missed call site is the whole incident.
Post-filtering an unfiltered search: it still leaks through counts and timing, and you paid for the wrong search.
Giving all 500 tenants a dedicated index — operations cost explodes with no risk-based justification.
Deriving tenant_id from anything the model produced instead of the authenticated request context.

followups.q: A tenant wants proof, not assurances. What do you hand them?
followups.a: The cross-tenant leakage suite results from CI, the single retrieval client code path, per-tenant trace records carrying tenant_id, the gateway residency check that blocks and alerts on violation, and the quarterly residency audit.

followups.q: Does the EU-only tenant change the isolation model?
followups.a: Yes — logical becomes physical. A regional data plane owns inference, vector DB, trace store and conversation memory; the global control plane holds config only. For an EU-ONLY tenant, regional failure returns 503 rather than failing over across the boundary.

followups.q: How do you know the filter is working today, before the redesign lands?
followups.a: Add the leakage probes now and run them hourly against production namespaces. Also grep every retrieval call site and count them — 11 of 13 is a number you can only quote because someone audited. Instrument filters-applied in the trace retrieval block.

drills.title: One tenant's load test is degrading everyone — design capacity fairness for shared inference
drills.problem: Aryaka runs a shared inference tier for 500 tenants: two self-hosted model pools plus a provider quota. Yesterday one tenant scripted 4,000 copilot queries in twenty minutes to benchmark the product. p95 for every other tenant went from 4s to 31s, three VIP accounts escalated, and the provider returned 429s for an hour after. Nobody was over any daily budget. You are asked to design capacity fairness: what you isolate, what you throttle, what VIP tenants get, and how the platform behaves in the next incident rather than the last one.
assesses: Separating capacity fairness from budget enforcement
Which quota dimension actually protects GPU and KV-cache memory
Bulkheading and per-tenant blast radius in a shared pool
Where the enforcement point lives as scale grows
Degradation that keeps a tenant served rather than rejected
skeleton: Diagnose precisely: this was a concurrency and TPM event, not a budget event, so cost ceilings would not have caught it.
Track four dimensions independently per tenant: RPS, tokens per minute, concurrent requests, daily cost ceiling.
Concurrency is the dimension that protects GPU and KV-cache memory; long AI requests make RPS a weak proxy.
Bulkhead the worker pool: a reserved share for VIP and internal traffic so normal-traffic saturation queues instead of starving.
Enforce atomically in Redis with Lua, sharded by tenant; never in application memory across pods.
Circuit-break per provider and per tool so one exhausted upstream does not cascade.
Degrade instead of rejecting: queue-and-async with a job id, then cheaper model, then cached response, always with Retry-After.
Differentiate the message — a tenant with budget hitting RPS must not be told budget exhausted.
Move enforcement to the gateway or mesh as volume grows, and reconcile counters hourly against billing ground truth.
numbers: The event: 4,000 requests in 20 minutes is ~3.3 RPS sustained, trivial by web standards but 4,000 concurrent-capable AI requests is the real load (issue 008, §5).
Enforcement scaling: Redis becomes the hot path around 1,000 RPS with 100 tenants; at 10,000 RPS the middleware moves to the gateway (issue 008, §5).
Bulkhead split to defend: 80% normal traffic, 20% reserved VIP, 10% internal tools (issue 003, §7).
Circuit thresholds: trip after 5 consecutive failures or 50% failure over 30s, half-open after 60s (issue 003, §7).
traps: Answering with RPS limits alone — asymmetric AI cost and 5-60 second requests make RPS the least protective dimension.
One global limit shared by all tenants, which turns any spike into everyone's outage.
Returning bare 429s to a paying tenant with budget remaining.
In-process counters in a multi-pod deployment, which diverge silently.

followups.q: A VIP tenant demands guaranteed capacity, not a reserved share. What do you offer?
followups.a: Reserved throughput at the provider plus a dedicated bulkhead and, past a threshold, dedicated self-hosted capacity. Above 10M calls a month capacity becomes the constraint anyway: multi-provider, reserved throughput, and an explicit brownout policy with an owner.

followups.q: How do you stop this being caught by a human next time?
followups.a: Cost is a reliability signal: page on 3x baseline in an hour, auto-degrade above 5x, and alert on concurrency saturation per tenant. The $40K incident had its alert paged four hours before anyone acted, which is a runbook failure, not a detection failure.

followups.q: Per-region or global quotas?
followups.a: Per-region for RPS because it is latency-sensitive; global with eventual consistency, accurate within 5-10 seconds, for daily cost ceilings. A single global Redis for everything adds 50-100ms to the hot path for accuracy nobody needs.

drills.title: Design an overnight batch re-triage of 40,000 backlogged alerts in a 6-hour window
drills.problem: Aryaka's NOC has 40,000 alerts from the last 30 days that were never triaged beyond auto-acknowledge. Management wants them re-triaged into outage, false positive, or maintenance so the team can find the systemic causes. The batch must finish inside a 6-hour maintenance window, must not touch the interactive copilot's provider quota, and has a hard budget of $4,000 for the whole run. Nothing is user-facing: no human waits at a keyboard. You are asked for the queue and worker design, the sizing arithmetic, and what happens when the window closes with work left.
assesses: Recognising a batch shape and dropping interactive-latency machinery
Capacity arithmetic tying throughput, concurrency and cost together
Isolating batch load from interactive quota
Designing for partial completion and resumability rather than all-or-nothing
Which steps need no model at all
skeleton: Reframe: this is throughput-bound and latency-tolerant, so optimise cost per successful triage, not p95.
Kill volume before any model call: dedupe and suppress with rules, then deterministic enrichment lookups.
Classify with a small model and structured output; escalate only low-confidence items to the frontier tier.
Queue with visibility timeout and dead-letter; workers are stateless, state and results persist per alert group.
Size workers from the window, not from intuition; cap concurrency to protect the interactive tenant's quota.
Separate quota pools: batch runs on its own key or self-hosted tier, bulkheaded from the copilot's capacity.
Checkpoint per alert group so a crash or window close resumes rather than restarts.
On window close, stop cleanly, report coverage, and requeue the remainder for the next window.
numbers: Dedupe first: T0 rules kill 60-80% of alert volume for free, so 40,000 becomes ~8,000-16,000 model-touched items (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §19).
Throughput: 12,000 items in 6 hours = 2,000/hour = ~0.56/sec; at 20s per item you need ~12 concurrent workers (0.56 x 20 = 11.2).
Cost: target under $0.10 per triage gives 12,000 x $0.10 = $1,200, inside the $4,000 budget with headroom for the frontier escalations (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §19).
Guardrails per item: max 8 tool calls, max $0.40, max 45s wall clock — the cap that bounds the tail (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §19).
traps: Reusing the interactive path unchanged: you pay frontier prices and starve the copilot's quota.
Unbounded parallelism to finish faster, which trips provider rate limits and turns into retry storms.
No dedupe stage, so 60-80% of the spend buys duplicate answers.
Treating an unfinished window as a failure instead of designing coverage reporting and resume.

followups.q: Halfway through, the classifier's confidence collapses on a whole alert class. What happens?
followups.a: Low confidence routes to a human queue and is logged for eval rather than guessed. If one class dominates the low-confidence bucket, pause that class, keep the rest running, and add the class to the gold set. Segment eval scores or the aggregate hides the collapse.

followups.q: Why not run this on the interactive stack at 3am when it is idle?
followups.a: Because idle capacity is not idle quota. Provider TPM and concurrency limits are shared, and one batch can drain the daily cost ceiling the interactive tenants depend on. Separate pools, separate ceilings, bulkheaded workers.

drills.title: Design the runbook corpus refresh pipeline: 40,000 pages, weekly churn, provenance required
drills.problem: The copilot retrieves from 40,000 Confluence pages, a git repo of device configs, and 90 days of resolved tickets. Roughly 400 pages change a week and superseded escalation procedures are still being retrieved with full confidence. Nobody owns corpus hygiene; two eval regressions last quarter turned out to be corpus changes, not model changes. You are asked for the refresh pipeline, how freshness and provenance are enforced at query time, and how the eval set stays calibrated when the corpus moves underneath it.
assesses: Treating retrieval quality as a pipeline with owners, not a database purchase
Freshness, versioning and effective-dating as retrieval-time filters
Corpus snapshot versioning tied to eval comparability
Incremental re-indexing and ingestion monitoring
Curation as a lever versus retriever tuning
skeleton: Frame it as a pipeline: parse, structure, chunk semantically, enrich metadata, embed, index, evaluate.
Chunk on structure — procedure, config stanza, table row — and attach the heading path to every chunk.
Separate retrieval text from display text: embed the enriched form, put the clean content in context.
Enrich metadata mandatorily: tenant, product, version, component, effective date, classification, source, permissions.
Filter on effective date at query time and boost recency; a superseded procedure retrieved confidently is an incident.
Hybrid retrieve broadly then rerank: error codes and CLI strings are exact-match problems.
Incremental re-index on change events with a freshness SLA and monitoring for stale, failed and duplicated ingests.
Stamp a corpus snapshot id in every trace and every eval run so results are comparable across time.
Alert when the corpus changes significantly, because the evals were calibrated against the old one.
Name an owner for corpus hygiene: dedupe, remove superseded, tag metadata — usually beats retriever tuning.
numbers: Gold set size: 100-300 representative support questions with expected document and expected section per question (doc: rag01 §13).
Retrieve broadly then narrow: k of 30-50 candidates, cross-encoder rerank, pass 3-5 into context (doc: agentic-ai-system-design-deep-dive §11).
Churn rate: 400 of 40,000 pages a week is 1% weekly, about 40% of the corpus a year — a freshness SLA is mandatory, not optional.
Eval-set retrofit costs 3 engineer-months versus 1 engineer-week for 50 examples growing at 5 a week (issue 008, §18).
traps: Answering with a vector database choice — buying one gets you approximately none of the way there.
Fixed 512-token chunking, which splits tables and separates headings from content.
Reporting an eval pass rate without the eval-set hash and corpus snapshot, so improvements are unfalsifiable.
Letting the vector store be the source of truth instead of preserving raw documents.

followups.q: Recall drops 18% after a refresh. How do you tell corpus from chunker from retriever?
followups.a: Freeze two of the three. Re-run the gold set against the previous corpus snapshot with the same chunker; if recall returns, it is corpus. Same corpus with the old chunker isolates chunking. Otherwise check hybrid fusion and reranker versions.

followups.q: Why hybrid rather than better embeddings?
followups.a: Because the domain is full of exact identifiers — IKE-001, UDP 4500, show vpn tunnel status, ticket ids. Dense vectors are good at concepts and bad at exact strings; in infrastructure domains lexical often beats pure vector and the hybrid beats both.

followups.q: Leadership asks why curation deserves headcount.
followups.a: A small clean corpus outperforms a large messy one. Morgan Stanley's vetted bounded corpus is the reference: dedupe, remove superseded documents, tag metadata. That effort typically beats the effort spent tuning the retriever, and it is the cheapest fix for confidently-wrong answers.

drills.title: Where does the budget object live, who may change it, and what does it log?
drills.problem: You run the agent platform for six product teams. Every team hardcoded max_iterations=10 as a round number. One team enforces limits in the system prompt with the line 'You have used 6 of your 10 allowed tool calls. Do not exceed 10.' A free-tier tenant's query and an enterprise customer's live incident get the identical envelope. Finance now wants per-tenant daily cost ceilings and an answer to 'which runs cost us money and finished nothing'. One team also wants to fan out to sub-agents and is worried a child will blow the parent's envelope. Design the budget as an object: where it lives, its fields, who configures it, and what it emits.
assesses: Whether budgets, permissions, and caps are harness state rather than prompt text
Knowledge that a cap is a backstop, not a plan, and that the firing dimension is the diagnostic
Per-tool caps and budget nesting for sub-agents
Whether they connect step caps to cost control via quadratic context
Multi-tenant configurability and where the ownership boundary sits
skeleton: Principle: the harness owns budgets, the model owns judgment.
Delete the prompt line — the model cannot count and can be argued out of a constraint.
Make Budget a typed object: max_steps, max_tokens, max_cost_usd, max_wall_clock_s, per-tool caps.
It exposes debit(), exhausted() returning which cap fired, and slice() for children.
Log the firing dimension in the trace: 'ran out of steps with 12% of cost spent' is actionable.
Per-tool caps are separate from total steps: read_file 30 times, send_email once.
Budgets nest and slice, so a sub-agent gets a fraction of the parent's envelope.
Budgets are per-tenant configurable — an enterprise incident is worth more compute than a free-tier query.
Step caps are a cost control too, because naive context growth is quadratic.
Budget on p95, not the mean, and chart termination reason alongside cost.
numbers: Why caps are cost controls: iteration 40 of a naive loop costs ~30× iteration 1 (~1.14M cumulative input tokens at 40 steps vs ~28k at 5) (doc §11).
Tail arithmetic to quote to finance: 93% × $0.08 + 7% × $2.40 = $0.242 blended, where the 7% tail is ~69% of the bill (doc §24).
Cap miscalibration read: exhausted() reporting the step cap while only ~12% of the cost budget was consumed means raise steps, not spend (doc §14).

Sub-agent slicing on my scenario: a parent with a 10-step / $0.25 envelope granting three children a 1/3 slice each caps child spend at ~$0.08 and keeps the parent whole. Assumption: an even three-way slice; real slices should be weighted by expected work.
traps: Enforcing caps in the prompt. It is the canonical anti-pattern; the model exceeds the limit and you learn nothing.
Reporting 'ran out of budget' without the dimension. Unactionable, and it hides that half your failures needed 12 steps and had cost budget to spare.
One global cap for all tenants. It underserves the incident that matters and overspends on the free-tier query.
Letting sub-agents draw from a shared pool. Without nesting and slicing a fan-out can blow the parent's envelope silently.
termdrops: budget as a first-class typed object
per-tool caps distinct from step caps

followups.q: A team says the step cap is causing failures. Do you raise it?
followups.a: Only after reading which cap fired and the cost consumed at termination. If steps fired with cost budget left, raise steps. If cost fired, the fix is tool-result summarization and compaction so late steps stop costing 30× early ones. Raising both blindly just buys a more expensive failure.

followups.q: Finance wants a hard daily ceiling per tenant. Any risk in that?
followups.a: Yes — a ceiling converts overspend into refusal, so it needs a defined degradation outcome, not a crash. I would make it a per-tenant configurable cap with a documented behaviour on breach, and track termination reason so 'ceiling hit' is distinguishable from 'agent gave up'.

followups.q: What do you put in the trace so the budget is debuggable a month later?
followups.a: Per run: the budget granted, every debit, the dimension that terminated it, and token counts attributed by context source — memory, retrieval, transcript, tool results. That last one turns 'the prompt got big' into 'memory retrieval is 60% of our context', which is a fixable statement.

drills.title: You track seventeen eval metrics. Which ones block a release, and why those?
drills.problem: You own the agent platform for six product teams shipping weekly in a multi-tenant service provider. The dashboard carries seventeen metrics, and releases are blocked on one composite: agent score at or above 87%. Last quarter two incidents shipped green — an approval bypass on a customer-facing change, and a latency regression that tripled P95 while the average barely moved. Teams complain that the gate is simultaneously too loose and too annoying, and one team has started shipping behind a feature flag to avoid it. A compliance audit lands in 90 days. Leadership wants fewer, sharper gates and a defensible appeal path.
assesses: Ability to classify metrics into zero-tolerance, thresholded and monitored-only
Understanding why aggregation hides safety failures
Knowing that pre-launch gates and canary catch different classes of regression
Organizational design: making a gate teams will not route around
Calibration discipline — targets from baseline, not copied from a table
skeleton: Kill the composite: 87% blended is exactly how a 1% safety violation disappears into a rounding error.
Three classes of metric: zero-tolerance blockers, thresholded blockers, and monitored-only signals.
Zero-tolerance, any occurrence blocks: policy violations, unauthorized actions, approval bypasses, cross-account data access.
Thresholded: task success >95%, tool selection >98%, tool argument >99%, valid transitions 100%, grounded claims >95%, recovery >90%.
Monitored-only: cost per successful task, tool and model calls per task, adoption and action rate — they inform, not block.
Add an explicit P95 latency gate against the SLA, since averages hid the 3x regression.
Gate per stratum, not aggregate: simple, medium, hard and adversarial pass rates reported separately.
Pre-launch gates catch known regressions; canary at 5% with auto-rollback catches the unknown ones. Require both.
Appeal path: thresholded gates can be waived by a named owner with an expiry date; zero-tolerance gates cannot.
Publish the baseline next to every target — these are starting points calibrated to risk, not industry standards.
numbers: How 87% happens: task 96, tool 99, grounding 95, latency 80, safety 99 averaged looks fine while safety's 1% is a live unauthorized action.
The production-ready conjunction to recite: safety violations = 0 AND policy bypasses = 0 AND task success >95% AND groundedness >95%.
Canary rule: 5% of traffic for 48 hours, auto-rollback if CSAT falls more than 0.3 below baseline, no overrides.
Model swap: 90/10 A/B for two weeks, roll to 50% after 7 flat-or-better days, roll back if any metric degrades more than 5%.
traps: Gating on all seventeen — six teams will route around a gate that fails weekly on cosmetics, as one already has.
Keeping the composite because leadership wants one number; give them an engineering view and a business view instead.
Quoting targets as industry standards rather than baselines calibrated to business criticality and risk.
Gating only pre-launch — the happy-path eval passed at 95% and still dropped CSAT to 3.2 from 4.5.

followups.q: A zero-tolerance gate fires on a false positive and blocks all six teams. Now what?
followups.a: Fix the evaluator, never the gate. Deterministic checks are debuggable in minutes: replay the trace, confirm the transition or approval assertion, add the case to the golden set. Waiving a zero-tolerance gate once teaches teams it is negotiable.

followups.q: How do these gates survive the compliance audit?
followups.a: The trace is the artifact: trace_id, case_id, agent, prompt and model version, per-step tool name, arguments, response, latency, error, plus per-dimension eval scores including the policy score. Approval-bypass rate of zero is only credible with a trace that shows the approval state.

followups.q: If a team has no gates at all today, which one do you install first?
followups.a: Approval bypass = 0. It is deterministic, cheap to compute from the state machine, needs no judge, and prevents the worst outcome — an irreversible customer-facing action taken without a human. Task success and grounding can wait a sprint.

drills.title: After compaction the agent re-ran an approach it had already rejected. Redesign compaction.
drills.problem: A config-remediation agent works inside a 200k-token window on multi-hour tasks. Compaction fires when the window is full, summarizing the transcript into a paragraph of prose. Last week a run tried a rollback path, found it unsafe, ruled it out, then hit compaction and re-attempted the same rollback — this time executing a write before a human caught it. The team also discards raw transcripts after compaction to save storage, so the post-incident review had only the summary. They want a compaction design they can defend to a change-advisory board. What do you build, and what do you never compact?
assesses: Whether compaction is treated as a designed context operation with a schema, not a prose summarizer
Knowledge of the specific post-compaction failure signature and its cause
Awareness that compaction is itself a model call that can hallucinate, and needs an eval
Separation of context operations from data retention and audit
Whether they consider delegation as an alternative before compacting at all
skeleton: Root cause: the reasoning that ruled out the rollback was summarized away.
Fix the trigger first: compact at 60–70% of the window, not at the limit.
Compaction needs headroom; hitting the ceiling mid-compaction is a hard failure.
Compact into a schema: goal verbatim, constraints, decisions with reasons, findings, current state, open questions.
Add the row teams miss: an explicit tried_and_failed list that survives every compaction.
Keep the last N turns verbatim — recency carries specifics summaries lose.
The raw transcript always goes to the trace; compaction is a context operation, never data deletion.
Eval compaction directly: run a task, compact, diff the compacted state against ground truth.
Expect prompt-cache invalidation at the boundary; that cost spike is cheaper than not compacting.
Then ask whether sub-agent delegation avoids the compaction entirely for this workload.
numbers: Trigger at 60–70% of a 200k window means compacting at roughly 120k–140k tokens, leaving ~60k of headroom for the compaction call itself (doc §12).
Why the window fills: naive accumulation is O(N²) — ~28k cumulative input tokens at 5 iterations, ~305k at 20, ~1.14M at 40 (doc §11).
Cheaper alternative to compaction: a bounded sub-loop burns ~30k tokens internally and returns a ~300-token findings object, so the parent pays for a short run (doc §13).
Ingestion discipline: summarize a 4,000-token tool response into a ~200-token structured extract, raw copy to the trace — a 20× reduction per observation (doc §11).
traps: Compacting into prose. A structured object is more reliably consumed, and it is inspectable and testable; a paragraph is neither.
Treating compaction as a storage decision. Dropping the raw transcript destroyed the incident review; compaction must never delete data.
Assuming compaction is safe because it is 'just summarization'. It is a model call, its errors are durable within the run and invisible afterwards.
Raising the window size as the fix. A bigger window delays the same failure and long contexts degrade accuracy anyway.
termdrops: keep the last N turns verbatim

followups.q: The change board asks how you prevent the write from executing at all next time.
followups.a: Two harness controls independent of compaction: a policy check inside the loop on every write call against the current declared state, and an idempotency key on tool execution so a repeated write is a no-op. The Replit deletion reading is exactly this — authorization evaluated per call, not at session start.

followups.q: How do you test a compaction change before shipping it?
followups.a: Its own eval suite: a set of tasks with known ground-truth state, compact mid-run, and score the compacted object field by field — goal preserved verbatim, constraints intact, tried_and_failed complete. Then deterministic replay of past runs through the new compactor at zero token cost for the harness logic.

followups.q: Your cost spikes at every compaction boundary. Is that acceptable?
followups.a: Yes, and I would label it. Compaction invalidates the prompt cache for that run by definition, so expect the spike. It is still cheaper than letting a quadratic transcript run to the window limit. What I would not accept is a harness that rewrites earlier messages, because that destroys the cache continuously.

drills.title: Leadership wants the agent to learn its own runbooks. What do you allow?
drills.problem: Your operations agent carries about 300 runbook procedures as markdown in git, human-authored and code-reviewed, loaded by progressive disclosure. A VP has seen a demo of an agent that saves successful behaviours as reusable skills and wants the same: after any successful run, the agent writes a new runbook and it is live immediately. Two facts complicate it. A meaningful share of runs terminate on the model declaring success, not on a verified check.
